# Look Before You Model {#sec-explore}

```{python}
#| label: ch9-setup
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from scripts import water as w
from scripts.figures import INK, MUTED, style
from scripts.scenes import tunja

A = w.A
raw = w.raw()
band = A.irca_band(raw["irca"]).astype(str).where(raw["irca"].notna(), "No IRCA")
order = ["No IRCA"] + A.IRCA_BANDS
tab = pd.crosstab(raw["zone"], band).reindex(columns=order, fill_value=0).reindex(["rural", "urban"])
pct = tab.div(tab.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100
rural_missing = f"{pct.loc['rural', 'No IRCA']:.0f}%"
urban_missing = f"{pct.loc['urban', 'No IRCA']:.0f}%"
rural_high = tab.loc["rural", ["High", "Unfit"]].sum() / tab.loc["rural", A.IRCA_BANDS].sum()
urban_high = tab.loc["urban", ["High", "Unfit"]].sum() / tab.loc["urban", A.IRCA_BANDS].sum()
med = raw.groupby(["year", "zone"])["irca"].median().unstack()
ZONE = {"urban": "#2f72b0", "rural": "#b07a14"}
tj = tunja(raw)
first, last = int(raw["year"].min()), int(raw["year"].max())
WORD = dict(enumerate(["zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight",
                       "nine", "ten", "eleven", "twelve", "thirteen", "fourteen", "fifteen"]))
drops = sorted(med["rural"].diff().nsmallest(2).index)       # the two sharpest falls
# Tunja: why it is a good case, from its rows.
tjr = tj["rows"]
munis = raw[raw["entity_type"] == "municipality"]
n_munis = munis["divipola"].nunique()
n_years = raw["year"].nunique()
rural_full = int(munis[munis["zone"] == "rural"].groupby("divipola")["irca"].count().eq(n_years).sum())
tj_full = bool(tjr["irca"].notna().all())
tj_rural = tjr[tjr["zone"] == "rural"].set_index("year")["irca"].sort_index()
tj_rural_high = A.irca_band(tj_rural).astype(str).eq("High")
tj_rural_high_to = int(tj_rural.index[tj_rural_high.cumprod().astype(bool)].max())  # first run
tj_urban_max = tjr.loc[tjr["zone"] == "urban", "irca"].max()
tj_zero = sorted(int(y) for y in tjr.loc[tjr["water_coverage_total"].eq(0), "year"].unique())
idf_last = int(raw.loc[raw["idf"].notna(), "year"].max())
idf_new_first = int(raw.loc[raw["idf_new"].notna(), "year"].min())


def spans(years) -> str:
    """[2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2019, 2020, 2022] -> "2014–2017, 2019, 2020 and 2022"."""
    ys, out = sorted(int(y) for y in years), []
    start = ys[0]
    for a, b in zip(ys, ys[1:] + [None]):
        if b != a + 1:
            out += [f"{start}–{a}"] if a - start > 1 else [str(y) for y in range(start, a + 1)]
            start = b
    return out[0] if len(out) == 1 else ", ".join(out[:-1]) + " and " + out[-1]


saber_years = spans(raw.loc[raw["saber11_mean"].notna(), "year"].unique())


def alt_text_holds(ok: bool, figure: str) -> None:
    """Alt texts and captions are static cell options, so they cannot quote computed values.
    Stop the render when the data no longer match what one says, so that it is rewritten."""
    if not ok:
        raise ValueError(f"the alt text of {figure} no longer matches the data: rewrite it")
```

Before any model, look at the data. Exploring tells you what a model will and will not be able
to see: which columns are sparse, which zones are never measured, and whether a series changes
level for reasons that have nothing to do with the thing it measures. None of that shows up as
an error. A clustering algorithm will happily group rows that have been made comparable only by
filling their gaps, and a chart of a series whose method changed will draw a trend that is not
there.

The water data hold two such surprises that a chart can show, and several more that show only
up close, in one place. For those, this chapter meets Tunja, the municipality the rest of the part
follows. Then the assistant builds the project's first page, `explore.qmd`, and you check it against
what you have already seen.

## What exploring is for {#sec-explore-what}

Four questions are worth answering before modelling any table, and this chapter asks each of
them of the water data:

1. **How big is it?** Rows and columns, and what one row is.
2. **What is missing, and where?** Missingness by column and by group (here, by zone).
3. **How are the key values distributed?** For IRCA, the count of rows in each risk band.
4. **How do they move over time?** For IRCA, its median by year and zone.

The answers decide what the analysis can claim. If one group is mostly missing, conclusions
about it rest on the minority that was measured, and that minority may not be typical.

## Rural: less data, more risk {#sec-water-bands}

```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-bands
#| fig-cap: "All rows, 2010–2023, by zone: no IRCA reported (hatched) and the Resolución 2115 risk band of the rest. Utility-supplied IRCA, INS open data (datos.gov.co nxt2-39c3)."
#| fig-alt: "Two horizontal stacked bars, urban and rural. The urban bar is mostly no-risk and low-risk IRCA with a small hatched no-data share. The rural bar is more than half hatched no-data, and the largest share of the rest is in the high-risk band."
#| classes: on-light
alt_text_holds((first, last) == (2010, 2023) and pct.loc["rural", "No IRCA"] > 50
               and pct.loc["urban", "No IRCA"] < 20 and pct.loc["urban", ["No risk", "Low"]].sum() > 50
               and tab.loc["rural", A.IRCA_BANDS].idxmax() == "High", "fig-wat-bands")
with style():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.6))
    left = np.zeros(2)
    cols = [A.NO_DATA_COLOR["light"]] + A.BAND_COLORS["light"]
    for b, c in zip(order, cols):
        nodata = b == "No IRCA"
        ax.barh(["rural", "urban"], pct[b], left=left, color=c, height=0.6, label=b,
                hatch=A.NO_DATA_HATCH if nodata else None,
                edgecolor=A.NO_DATA_EDGE["light"] if nodata else "white", linewidth=0 if nodata else 1)
        left += pct[b].to_numpy()
    ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
    ax.set_xlabel("Share of rows (%)")
    ax.legend(ncol=3, loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, 1.02), fontsize=9, handlelength=1.2)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

Side by side, @fig-wat-bands shows all `{python} w.fmt(len(raw))` rows. `{python} rural_missing` of
rural rows have no IRCA at all, against `{python} urban_missing` of urban rows, because many rural
systems are never sampled, or are not run by a utility and so fall outside the utility-supplied
table. Among the rural rows that do have a value,
`{python} f"{rural_high:.0%}"` fall in the high or unfit bands, against `{python} f"{urban_high:.0%}"`
of urban rows.

The two facts compound, in the worst direction: the zones whose scores are worse are also the
ones least often scored. The gaps are not missing at random: they depend on zone, and perhaps on
the risk itself. Any
analysis that drops the rows without IRCA, as Part III's must, describes *sampled* rural systems
only, and should say so.

```{python}
#| label: fig-wat-years
#| fig-cap: "Median utility-supplied IRCA by year and zone, 2010–2023, over the rows that report one."
#| fig-alt: "Two lines over the years 2010 to 2023. The urban median is low and falls gently, from the low-risk band in the early years to under 5 from the middle of the decade. The rural median is far higher and nearly flat until 2015, then falls sharply in 2016 and again in 2020, ending in the low-risk band."
#| classes: on-light
alt_text_holds((first, last) == (2010, 2023) and drops == [2016, 2020]
               and str(A.irca_band(med["rural"].iloc[[-1]]).iloc[0]) == "Low", "fig-wat-years")
with style():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.8))
    for z in ("rural", "urban"):
        ax.plot(med.index, med[z], marker="o", ms=4, color=ZONE[z], label=z)
    ax.set_ylabel("Median IRCA")
    ax.set_xticks(med.index[::2])
    ax.legend(loc="upper right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

The fourth question matters, as @fig-wat-years shows. The rural median drops sharply in
`{python} drops[0]` and again in `{python} drops[1]`. That could be an improvement in rural water, or
a change in which systems were sampled; the data's README warns that the `{python} drops[1]` drop may
reflect sampling, and the open data cannot tell the two apart. An analysis that compares years
should not read the drop as progress without evidence from outside the table.

## One municipality to follow: Tunja {#sec-tunja}

Aggregates hide the details that make a variable trustworthy or not, so from here on this part
follows one municipality through every step. Tunja, the capital of Boyacá department, is a good case
for three reasons in its rows. As a department capital, it carries the coverage caveat that every
capital does. Unlike most municipalities, it has an IRCA for both zones in every year: only
`{python} w.fmt(rural_full)` of the `{python} w.fmt(n_munis)` municipalities have one for their rural
zone in all `{python} WORD[n_years]` years, so the analysis will never lose Tunja for want of a
score. And its two zones differ: its rural water scored in the high-risk band every year from
`{python} first` to `{python} tj_rural_high_to`, while its urban water never scored above
`{python} f"{tj_urban_max:.1f}"`.

Tunja has `{python} len(tjr)` rows, `{python} WORD[tjr["zone"].nunique()]` zones over
`{python} WORD[tjr["year"].nunique()]` years. Looking at them one variable at a time shows several of
the README's caveats in a single place (@fig-tunja).

::: {.content-visible when-format="html:js"}
::: {#fig-tunja}
```{python}
#| output: asis
print(tj["html"])
```

Tunja's `{python} len(tjr)` rows, from `water_municipal.csv`. Pick a view (the data, a summary, a distribution, a time series or a scatter plot), then a variable and a zone. Variables that repeat the same value in both zone rows are municipal and are counted once.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="epub"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-tunja
#| fig-cap: "Tunja, 2010–2023: utility-supplied IRCA by zone (left) and the municipality's aqueduct coverage (right), where a hollow point is a value reported as 0. From `water_municipal.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Two small charts. Left: Tunja's urban IRCA is in the low-risk band in the first two years and near zero after that, while its rural IRCA is much higher, in the high-risk band until 2014, and falls to the low and medium bands from 2016. Right: the municipality's aqueduct coverage moves between about 60 and 100 percent, with a hollow point at 0 in the one year reported as 0, which probably means not reported rather than no service."
#| classes: on-light
alt_text_holds((first, last) == (2010, 2023) and tj_full and tj_rural_high_to == 2014
               and len(tj_zero) == 1, "fig-tunja")
p_irca = tj["pivot"]["irca"]
p_cov = tj["pivot"]["water_coverage_total"]["urban"]
with style():
    fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.0, 2.8))
    for z in ("urban", "rural"):
        a1.plot(p_irca.index, p_irca[z], marker="o", ms=4, color=ZONE[z], label=z)
    a1.set_title("IRCA, utility-supplied")
    a1.legend(fontsize=9)
    zero = p_cov.eq(0)
    a2.plot(p_cov.index, p_cov.where(~zero), marker="o", ms=4, color=MUTED)
    a2.scatter(p_cov.index[zero], p_cov[zero], s=30, facecolors="none", edgecolors=MUTED, linewidths=1.5)
    a2.set_title("Aqueduct coverage (%)")
    for a in (a1, a2):
        a.set_xticks([2010, 2014, 2018, 2022])
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

::: {.live-link}
Explore all `{python} WORD[len(tj["pivot"])]` of Tunja's variables in the website edition, at
<https://project-delphi.github.io/quarto-workshop/book/chapters/09-explore.html#sec-tunja>,
or scan: ![QR code for the Tunja explorer in the website edition.](../media/qr/tunja.png){.qr}

:::

Five things are worth finding. Because Tunja is a department capital, its coverage has no urban
and rural split, so the explorer uses the municipality's total. That total is reported as exactly 0
in `{python} spans(tj_zero)`, which beside its neighbouring years probably means "not reported"
rather than "no service"; such points are drawn hollow. The fiscal index `idf` ends in
`{python} idf_last` and `idf_new` starts there, on a different scale, so the two must never be joined
into one line. Infant mortality changes method in 2017, so its apparent drop that year cannot be
read as an improvement. And Saber 11 exists only for `{python} saber_years`.

::: practice
Summaries in the explorer never pool the two zones. Averaging the small rural population's values
with the much larger urban population's would describe neither. The same caution applies to every
comparison in this part: compare like with like, and say which rows a number comes from.
:::

## The first page: `explore.qmd` {#sec-explore-do}

::: {.prompt}
```default
Read data/README.md. Create explore.qmd from data/water_municipal.csv (divipola as text): rows and columns, % missing per column by `zone`, IRCA counts by Resolución 2115 band and `zone`, and median IRCA by `year` and `zone`, labelled utility-supplied (prestadores). Render it; report errors.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
writes `explore.qmd` · `uv run quarto render explore.qmd`
:::

::: {.you}
open `explore.html` in your browser
:::

"divipola as text" matters: the codes have leading zeros (`05001` is Medellín), and a code read as a
number loses them, and with them the join to any other table.

::: pitfall
Check the missingness table before trusting the page. If `irca` is not much sparser in rural rows
than in urban ones, the assistant probably counted the wrong column, or counted rows rather than
values. You now know the answer the table should give (@fig-wat-bands), which is exactly what makes
the check possible.
:::

::: tryit
Run the prompt and read the page.

::: done
`explore.html` shows rows and columns, missing values by zone, and IRCA by band, zone and year for
`{python} first`–`{python} last`.
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

Explore before you model: size, missingness by group, distributions and trends over time. In the
water data, rural rows are mostly unmeasured and, where measured, far riskier, so any analysis of
measured rows describes sampled systems only. The rural median IRCA falls sharply in
`{python} drops[0]` and `{python} drops[1]`, which the data alone cannot distinguish from a change in
sampling. Tunja, the department capital this part follows, shows the README's caveats in practice:
no zone split for capitals, a zero that probably means "not reported", two fiscal indices on
different scales, and a method change in infant mortality. Read codes as text, and check each
summary against what you already know it should say. Seeing the gaps is not the same as deciding
what to do about them: the next chapter decides which rows and numbers the clustering will see, and
counts what each decision costs.
